newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says no problems between Italy and Germany.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says no problems between Italy and Germany.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Friday there were no bilateral problems between Germany and Italy, seeking to calm speculation of a rift over whether Italy can be among the first nations to adopt Europe's new currency.
But Kohl said the unemployment situation in Germany, where the jobless rate on Thursday reached a post-war record of 12.2 percent, and in Italy were "unacceptable".

"There are essentially no areas in which bilateral difficulties come into question and we are both on the way to build Europe," Kohl told a news conference after a one-day meeting with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Kohl said Italy and Germany were committed to sticking to the Maastricht Treaty criteria and the timetable laid out in the doucment for membership in the new currency, which will be called the euro and is slated to take effect in January 1999.
"We want to meet the deadline and we also want to meet the critiera," Kohl said.

Kohl said Germany would not participate in making judgment on who will join currency union, noting Germany itself had much work ahead and would make all efforts to stick to all of the criteria that must be met for Economic and Monetary Union.
But he said Germany could miss fulfiling Maastricht Treaty criteria without taking political steps.

"Now it is a question for everyone to do their homework. The fact that now people are already making judgments or giving marks to countries a full year before the decision will be taken, I view as absolutely unacceptable. That is wrong."
"We know that even Germany has a tough job ahead to be able to present itself to fulfil the treaty requirements next spring."
